title: Embedding Formative Assessment https://www.dropbox.com/scl/fi/kmi7g0pktnax4s4j9r418/EFA_QRG_10-04-2016.pdf
author: Craig Barton
summary: This Tips for Teachers research summary covers an excerpt from Dylan Wiliam and Siobhan Leahy's book Embedding Formative Assessment, which distills classroom formative assessment into five practical strategies teachers can build into daily practice. The five strategies are: clarifying and sharing learning intentions and success criteria; engineering discussions and activities that surface evidence of learning; giving feedback that moves learning forward; activating students as learning resources for each other through peer feedback; and activating students as owners of their own learning through self-assessment. Barton's summary emphasises the practical techniques attached to each strategy — planning questions in advance, using all-student response systems, giving thinking time, and treating self-assessment as a routine part of classwork rather than an occasional add-on. A recurring thread is that feedback should require more cognitive work from the student receiving it than from the teacher giving it, and should point forward to the next step rather than simply evaluate the last one. The excerpt's underlying philosophy, captured in Wiliam's own framing, is that learning is something students do for themselves — the teacher's job is to engineer the environment and interactions that make that learning happen, not to transmit it directly.
points: Feedback should be 'more work for the recipient than the donor' — actionable and specific enough that the student, not the teacher, does the cognitive work of closing the gap.

Formative assessment is broken into five concrete, trainable strategies rather than a vague disposition: clarify learning intentions, engineer evidence-eliciting activities, give forward-looking feedback, activate peer feedback, and activate self-assessment.
Self-assessment should be a routine, built-in part of classwork — not an occasional bolt-on — and can be used practically to group students for instruction.

Practical technique-level advice (planning questions in advance, all-student response systems, deliberate thinking time) is treated as inseparable from the higher-level strategies, not optional extras.

The philosophy underpinning the whole framework is captured in Wiliam and Leahy's own line that only learners create learning — the teacher's role is to engineer the environment, not transmit the content directly.
quotes: This excerpt from Embedding Formative Assessment by Wiliam and Leahy outlines five key strategies for effective formative assessment.
Strategy 3 details providing feedback that promotes student progress.
Teachers should provide feedback that moves learners forward. This means that feedback should be specific, timely, and actionable. It should also be more work for the recipient than the donor.
Teachers should activate students as learning resources for one another.
Teachers should activate students as owners of their own learning.
Stress that smart is not something you are but rather something you get. Focus feedback on what's next, not what's past.
Only learners create learning. Teachers create environments within which students learn.
